name: NTA Analysis Workflow — Descriptive, Diagnostic, Predictive, Prescriptive
description: Network Traffic Analysis (NTA) follows a 4-phase framework: Descriptive (what happened), Diagnostic (why it happened), Predictive (what might happen), Prescriptive (what to do). The 8-step practical workflow covers everything from capture setup to IOC extraction. Understanding which dependencies to capture (host-to-host, unique events, patterns) drives the whole analysis. Also covers the guided lab scenario (netcat shell + rogue admin user creation).
source: CDSA Module 07: Intro to Network Traffic Analysis
notes:
=== NTA ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK (4 PHASES) ===

[1] Descriptive Analysis
  → What happened?
  → Identify: what traffic occurred, which hosts communicated, what data was exchanged
  → Tools: tcpdump, Wireshark Packet List, basic display filters
  → Questions: What IPs are talking? On what ports? When? How much data?

[2] Diagnostic Analysis
  → Why did it happen?
  → Investigate anomalies, compare baseline vs observed
  → Tools: Follow Stream, Wireshark statistics, correlation with logs
  → Questions: Why is host X talking to this external IP? Is this normal?

[3] Predictive Analysis
  → What might happen next?
  → Pattern recognition, threat intel correlation
  → Tools: threat intel lookups, pattern matching, IOC extraction
  → Questions: If this is C2, what's the next stage? Data exfil? Lateral movement?

[4] Prescriptive Analysis
  → What should we do?
  → Actionable response: block IPs, isolate hosts, create detection rules
  → Output: firewall rules, IDS signatures, incident report, remediation steps

=== 8-STEP NTA WORKFLOW ===

Step 1 — Ingest Traffic
  → Decide: live capture or PCAP file
  → Live: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap
  → Use capture filters to reduce volume if interface is noisy
  → Tip: capture from a span port or tap — not the analyst's own machine

Step 2 — Define Scope
  → What are you looking for? Specific host? Protocol? Time window?
  → Set up display filters in Wireshark before drilling down
  → Ask: is this a targeted investigation or broad hunt?

Step 3 — Capture Dependencies (3 key views)
  A. Host-to-Host Conversations
     → Wireshark: Statistics → Conversations → TCP tab
     → Shows all pairs of talking hosts, bytes exchanged, packet counts
     → Spot: unexpected external connections, high volume transfers

  B. Unique Traffic Events
     → Look for unusual protocols, port numbers, or rare endpoints
     → Wireshark: Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy
     → Spot: TOR, IRC, non-standard ports, DNS over non-53

  C. Patterns
     → Repeating connections at regular intervals → beaconing (C2)
     → Large outbound transfers → data exfiltration
     → Many hosts connecting to single destination → DDoS or scanning
     → New admin protocols (RDP, SSH, WinRM) to sensitive hosts

Step 4 — Apply Filters to Reduce Noise
  → Exclude known-good traffic: not arp, not dns (if noise), not broadcast
  → Wireshark coloring rules highlight suspicious protocols in red
  → Focus on: tcp port 4444, unusual outbound HTTP/S, non-standard services

Step 5 — Examine Interesting Flows
  → Right-click suspicious packet → Follow → TCP Stream
  → Read protocol exchanges: look for commands, credentials, file names
  → Check timestamps: night/weekend activity by internal hosts = suspicious

Step 6 — Extract IOCs
  → IPs, domains, ports, user agents, file hashes from object exports
  → Commands seen in plaintext streams (Telnet, FTP, HTTP)
  → File names from FTP RETR/STOR, HTTP GET URIs
  → Credentials from cleartext protocols

Step 7 — Correlate with Other Data
  → Match IPs against threat intel feeds, SIEM logs, DNS logs
  → Correlate timestamps with endpoint events (process creation, logon events)
  → Wireshark time + SIEM time must align (check timezone offsets)

Step 8 — Document & Report
  → Note: what was found, packet numbers, timestamps, stream numbers
  → Export: PCAP segments, exported objects, screenshots of Follow Stream
  → Write: executive summary + technical findings + IOCs

=== KEY TRAFFIC PATTERNS TO HUNT ===

Beaconing (C2 check-in):
  → Regular intervals (every 30s, 60s, 5min) to same external IP
  → Small fixed-size packets
  → Filter: ip.dst == <SUSPICIOUS_IP> → sort by time → look for regularity

Data Exfiltration:
  → Large outbound transfers to unknown external IP
  → High byte count in Wireshark Conversations → Endpoints
  → DNS exfil: unusually long DNS queries or high-volume DNS to single resolver

Port Scanning:
  → Many TCP RST responses from target host
  → Lots of SYN packets from one source with no follow-up SYN-ACK
  → Filter: tcp[13] &2 != 0 (SYN packets) then look for patterns

Lateral Movement:
  → RDP (3389), SMB (445), WinRM (5985), SSH (22) between internal hosts
  → Auth-related traffic from unexpected sources
  → New connections using service accounts on non-standard times

=== GUIDED LAB: NETCAT SHELL INVESTIGATION ===
The M07 guided lab captures an attacker:
  1. Gaining a reverse shell via netcat on port 4444
  2. Running net user hacker /add
  3. Running net localgroup administrators hacker /add

Investigation approach:
  → Display filter: tcp.port == 4444
  → Follow TCP Stream → see bash/cmd commands in plaintext
  → Extract commands: net user, net localgroup → IOCs for incident report
  → Note: port 4444 = common netcat default — always alert-worthy

Expected stream contents show:
  → Commands typed by attacker (red in stream)
  → System responses (blue in stream)
  → Evidence of user creation and privilege escalation

=== TRAFFIC CAPTURE DEPENDENCIES TABLE ===
What to capture | Why | How
Host-to-host    | Find who's talking | Statistics → Conversations
Protocol use    | Detect unusual protocols | Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy
Volume by host  | Find exfil candidates | Statistics → Endpoints → Bytes column
DNS queries     | Detect C2 domains | dns filter + unique dst IPs
HTTP URIs       | Detect downloads/C2 | http.request.method==GET + follow stream
Auth traffic    | Lateral movement | tcp.port in {22,445,3389,5985}
Small-pkt floods | Scanning/DDoS | less 64 + Statistics → Conversations
